statement: In triangle $ABC$, the point $D$ lies on side $BC$ so that $BD = DA = AC$. Angle $BAC$ is $99^\circ$. What is the size of angle $ABC$?

choices.misconception: I assumed the three equal lengths split the $99^\circ$ angle at $A$ into three equal parts of $33^\circ$.
I assumed triangle $ABC$ itself is isosceles and split the remaining $81^\circ$ equally between $B$ and $C$.
I worked out the angle at $C$, which is $54^\circ$, and gave that instead of the angle at $B$.
I found $180^\circ - 99^\circ = 81^\circ$, which is the angles at $B$ and $C$ together, and gave it as the angle at $B$.

hints: Draw it, and mark the two isosceles triangles.
Call angle $ABC$ $x$. Triangle $ABD$ has $DB = DA$, and triangle $ADC$ has $AD = AC$. Use the exterior angle at $D$ to write every angle in terms of $x$.
Angle $BAD = x$, so the exterior angle $ADC = 2x$, and then angle $ACD = 2x$ too. Angle $DAC = 180^\circ - 4x$, so angle $BAC = x + (180^\circ - 4x)$.

solutions.reliable: Let angle $ABC = x$. In triangle $ABD$, $DB = DA$, so angle $BAD = x$. Angle $ADC$ is an exterior angle of triangle $ABD$, so it equals $x + x = 2x$. In triangle $ADC$, $AD = AC$, so angle $ACD$ equals angle $ADC$, which is $2x$, and angle $DAC = 180^\circ - 4x$. Then angle $BAC = x + (180^\circ - 4x) = 180^\circ - 3x = 99^\circ$, so $x = 27^\circ$. Check: the angles of triangle $ABC$ are $99^\circ$, $27^\circ$ and $54^\circ$, which add to $180^\circ$, and angle $DAC = 72^\circ$ is positive, so $D$ really lies on side $BC$. The transferable idea: in a chain of isosceles triangles, name one angle and let the exterior angle rule carry it along the chain.
solutions.elegant: The chain shows that angle $C$ is twice angle $B$: the exterior angle at $D$ is $2x$, and triangle $ADC$ copies it to $C$. The angle sum of triangle $ABC$ then gives $99^\circ + x + 2x = 180^\circ$, so $x = 27^\circ$.

whyOnTest: Two isosceles triangles hide inside one triangle; drawing it and following the exterior angle along the chain turns three equal lengths into one equation.
